title: The hierarchical lattice
subtitle: An ultrametric group whose blocks fall into L^d congruent children.
summary: The hierarchical lattice is the direct sum of countably many copies of (Z/LZ)^d, with an ultrametric whose balls have exactly L^(dn) points. Each ball splits into L^d congruent children, every pair of vertices in different children of a ball sits at the top distance of that ball, and power kernels are summable exactly when their exponent exceeds the dimension. These three facts are what make block decimation close on one-variable laws.
text:
The hierarchical lattice $\mathbb H^d_L$ is the abelian group of finite sequences with entries in $(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$, carrying the ultrametric in which two vertices are at distance $L^k$ when the last coordinate at which they differ is the $k$-th. Its balls are nested subgroups, of exactly $L^{dn}$ vertices at radius $L^n$, and each ball splits into $L^d$ congruent children. Every pair of vertices in different children of a ball lies at the top distance of that ball, so a coupling that charges each pair according to its distance charges all pairs between two children at one rate, which depends only on the two block sums. This is the structure that makes block decimation an exact operation on a single variable, and it is why the model appears throughout the rigorous theory of the renormalisation group [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. The lattice was introduced by Dyson (1969) as a one-dimensional model with long-range couplings in which a phase transition can be proved [@dyson-1969], and the group-theoretic description used here, with balls as cosets of nested subgroups, is the form in which the renormalisation group is usually set up [@bleher-sinai-1973]. A power kernel $\lVert xVert^{-d-\alpha}$ is summable exactly when $\alpha>0$, so the model with such a kernel is a long-range spin system with a finite interaction range in the only sense that matters: the total intensity at each vertex is finite. Two conventions are worth fixing at the outset. The dimension enters the lattice only through the block volume $m=L^d$ and the decay ratio $\lambda=L^{d+\alpha}=mL^{\alpha}$; any integer $m\geq2$ and any ratio $\lambda>m$ arise from some pair $(d,\alpha)$ once a scale $L$ is chosen. And the lattice is a group, so distances are translation invariant and every vertex looks like the origin. title: The isometries of the hierarchical lattice
subtitle: Why any two pairs at the same level are the same pair, and why block sums of a block are exchangeable.
summary: Translations and coordinate-wise bijections are isometries of the hierarchical lattice, and together they act transitively on ordered pairs at each level. Three statements that other articles use as "by symmetry" follow: a radial kernel gives a radial two-point function, the block sums of a block are exchangeable, and conditional expectations given the block sums are constant on the vertices of a child. A bijection that preserves the level of every vertex need not be an isometry, so the criterion has content.
text: Five articles in this wiki reason "by symmetry", and this article supplies the symmetry. The statements are that the two-point function of a radial kernel depends only on the distance; that the block sums of the children of a block are exchangeable; and that a conditional expectation given those block sums is constant over the vertices of a child. Each is true, and each follows from the same two facts: translations are isometries, and so are bijections that act on each coordinate separately. Together they move any ordered pair of vertices at a given level onto any other such pair. The last of the three is the one that does real work. In the Gaussian two-point computation the conditional expectation of a single spin given the block sums is replaced by the block sum divided by the size of the block; in the percolation article the level isometries convert an averaged bound into a pointwise one; and in the vector model it is exchangeability of the child sums that reduces the recursion to the law of one block sum, with all components moving together. Without a transitivity statement each of those steps is an assertion about a picture. One caution organises the proofs. Preserving the level of every vertex is strictly weaker than being an isometry: on a block of eight vertices a transposition of two vertices of level three preserves all vertex levels and changes the level of a pair. The example is given below, and it is the reason the theorem is about pairs. Definitions and setting # A bijection $\phi:\mathbb H^d_L\to\mathbb H^d_L$ is an isometry if $\lVert\phi(x)-\phi(y)\rVert=\lVert x-y\rVert$ for all $x,y$, equivalently if $\operatorname{lev}(\phi(x)-\phi(y))=\operatorname{lev}(x-y)$. Write $\operatorname{Isom}$ for the set of isometries; it is a group under composition, and it contains the translations $\tau_v(x)=x+v$ for $v\in\mathbb H^d_L$. For $a\in A$ let $\psi_a$ be the map that acts on each coordinate separately by a bijection of $A$: if $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots)$ is a sequence of bijections of $A$, then $\psi_\sigma(x)^{(i)}=\sigma_i(x^{(i)})$ for every $i$. These are the coordinate-wise bijections . Two families of isometries # Translations are isometries, and so is every coordinate-wise bijection. Consequently, for each $n\geq0$ and every pair of ordered pairs $(x,y)$, $(x',y')$ with $\operatorname{lev}(y-x)=\operatorname{lev}(y'-x')=n$, there is an isometry $\phi$ with $\phi(x)=x'$ and $\phi(y)=y'$. For a coordinate-wise bijection, the coordinates at which $\psi_\sigma(x)$ and $\psi_\sigma(y)$ differ are exactly the coordinates at which $x$ and $y$ differ: if $x^{(i)}\neq y^{(i)}$ then $\sigma_i(x^{(i)})\neq\sigma_i(y^{(i)})$ because $\sigma_i$ is injective, and if $x^{(i)}=y^{(i)}$ then the images are equal. The set of indices at which two vertices differ is therefore preserved, so its maximum is preserved, which is the level. For transitivity, let $x,y$ have $y-x=z$ of level $n$, and let $x',y'$ have $y'-x'=z'$ of level $n$. Translate by $-x$: the pair becomes $(0,z)$. By the previous paragraph, choose bijections $\sigma_i$ of $A$ with $\sigma_i(z^{(i)})=z'^{(i)}$ for $i\leq n$ and arbitrary for $i>n$ (possible because $A$ is a set and $\sigma_i$ is only required to take one prescribed value); the corresponding coordinate-wise bijection fixes $0$ and sends $z$ to $z'$. Composing with the translation by $x'$ gives an isometry taking $(x,y)$ to $(x',y')$. The proof uses no structure of $A$ beyond its cardinality, so the statement holds for the coefficient group $\mathbb Z^d$ as well, where the lattice is the direct sum of copies of $\mathbb Z^d$: the levels are unaffected. title: Hierarchical spin systems and decimation
subtitle: The block spin of a hierarchical model is distributed as a functional of independent copies of the block spin one scale down.
summary: A spin system on the hierarchical lattice with couplings constant on levels has a Hamiltonian that splits into the Hamiltonians of its children plus one interaction between their sums. Consequently the partition function and the law of a block spin are recovered from the law one scale down by an explicit operation, the free energy has an exact recursion, and the whole renormalisation group is a recursion on one-variable laws.
text: A hierarchical spin system is a spin model on $\mathbb H^d_L$ whose coupling between two vertices is a function of their level alone, so that the coupling at level $k$ has one value $J_k=JL^{-(d+\alpha)k}$. Its energy on a block splits exactly into the energies of the children of that block plus a single interaction between the child sums: pairs inside a child are at levels below the top, pairs in different children are all at the top level, and no pair inside the block is at a level above it. The partition function therefore factorises, and the law of a block spin is the image of the law one scale down under an explicit operation — block decimation — which acts on the single variable $\sum_{x\in\text{child}}\sigma_x$. This article states that identity, its iterates, and the free energy recursion that follows; the operation itself is studied in the next article and solved exactly in the Gaussian case . The identity is what is special about the lattice: on $\mathbb Z^d$ a decimation step produces an interaction that depends on the shape of the boundary between blocks, whereas here it produces one number per block. The structure is Dyson's (1969), who introduced the hierarchical approximation to prove a phase transition for power-law couplings [@dyson-1969], and it is the setting of the renormalisation analysis of Bleher and Sinai [@bleher-sinai-1973]. Only free boundary conditions are used, so every object below is finite-dimensional and every identity is exact at finite volume. title: The infinite-volume limit
subtitle: Finite-volume measures, the boundary field of a block, and which limits are Gibbs measures.
summary: The decimation identity is finite-volume, but the two-point function, the phase and the exponents are infinite-volume objects. This article takes the limit: configurations form a compact space, the boundary field of a block decays at rate L^{-alpha n} while its total energy grows like L^{(d-alpha)n}, the conditional law of a finite region is Lipschitz in that field, and consequently every limit point of the finite-volume measures is a Gibbs measure in the sense of Dobrushin, Lanford and Ruelle. Every such limit point of the free-boundary measures is invariant under translations and coordinate-wise bijections, so its two-point function depends on the level alone.
text:
Every identity in the decimation article is finite-volume and exact, and that is deliberate: the renormalisation group acts on the law of a block spin of a block, and a block never needs the lattice. But the objects the rest of the wiki measures are not finite-volume objects. The two-point function $	au_ eta(x,y)$ of the exponent article , the phase that the intensity selects, and the statement that $	au_ eta$ depends on the level alone are all statements about a measure on the whole lattice, and the lattice is infinite. This article supplies the passage. Three things are proved and nothing more is assumed: that the finite-volume measures have limit points, that every limit point satisfies the defining property of a Gibbs measure — the conditional law of a finite region given the rest of the configuration, which is the one condition that survives the limit — and that a limit point of the free-boundary measures inherits the lattice symmetry, so its two-point function is radial. What the limit is , whether it is unique, and whether the model is magnetised are questions of a different order: the last section of this article says which of them this argument does not touch, and the next one answers them for ferromagnetic couplings, in the form of the sign of a single number. The passage needs one arithmetic input, and it is the reason the article belongs to the first part. title: Ultrametric block systems and the p-adic models
subtitle: What the recursion actually needs, and how little of it is specific to the hierarchical lattice.
summary: The decimation recursion uses only a nested system of blocks with a constant number of children per block. Any ultrametric group with such a system carries the same model, the same map and the same exponents: the p-adic integers with their balls, the hierarchical lattice with its subgroups, and their variants. The child decomposition and the decimation identity are proved here in that generality, and the one place where the compact and discrete cases differ is isolated.
text:
Every proof in this wiki about decimation uses exactly two facts: that the blocks of a fixed level are the cosets of a subgroup, and that each block has the same number $m$ of children. Nothing else about the hierarchical lattice is used: not the direct-sum construction, not countability, not the arithmetic of $(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d$. This article states the construction for an arbitrary abelian group with a nested block system and proves the two structural results in that generality; the decimation identity , the map and the exponent dictionary then apply verbatim. The standard compact example is the ring of p-adic integers $\mathbb Z_p$ with the balls of the p-adic metric, which are the cosets of $p^n\mathbb Z_p$: each ball has exactly $p$ children, at every scale, forever. The models on $\mathbb Z_p$ are used in the renormalisation-group approach to conformal field theory, where the exactness of the block structure is worth the loss of translation invariance in the Euclidean sense [@abdesselam-2018]. The one point at which the two settings differ is the meaning of the volume of a block: a coset of $\Lambda_n$ in the hierarchical lattice is a finite set and its volume is its cardinality, while a ball in $\mathbb Z_p$ is uncountable and its volume is its Haar measure. The recursion sees only the ratio of the volumes of a block and its child, which is $m$ in both cases, so the two models have the same renormalisation group. The block at $x$ of level $n$ is the coset $x+G_n$; the children of a block $x+G_n$ are its cosets of $G_{n+1}$. Vertices at level $n$ are those in $G_n\setminus G_{n-1}$, and the shell at level $n$ is $G_n\setminus G_{n-1}$. Two examples carry the subject. For the hierarchical lattice $\mathbb H^d_L$ one takes $G_n=\Lambda_n$, the sequences supported on the first $n$ coordinates, and $m=L^d$; the blocks are finite and the volumes are cardinalities $m^n$. title: The magnetised phase, and what monotonicity gives
subtitle: Two extremal states, the order parameter, and why the FKG inequality cannot locate the threshold.
summary: For ferromagnetic couplings the FKG inequality makes the Gibbs measures of the hierarchical Ising model a stochastically ordered family with a largest and a smallest element: the monotone limits of the plus and minus boundary conditions. The order parameter M of the plus state is positive exactly when the Gibbs measure is not unique, and it equals the block average of that state at every finite volume; a nondegenerate limit of block averages is impossible when M vanishes, so the trichotomy's block spin and the order parameter carry the same information. Correlations under the plus state dominate M squared, so a magnetised phase has infinite susceptibility, and M is at most tanh of beta over the Gaussian critical intensity, which is the only bound on its size that monotonicity gives. The arguments are insensitive to the intensity, so the location of the threshold is not a monotonicity statement: it is the branch of the recursion's trichotomy, which is where Bleher and Sinai's analysis enters.
text:
The previous article showed that the free-boundary measures have limit points and that these are Gibbs measures, but it said nothing about how many Gibbs measures there are. For a ferromagnetic model the answer has a shape, and the shape costs nothing: the Gibbs measures are stochastically ordered, there is a smallest and a largest, and the model is in one phase exactly when the two coincide. All of that follows from the FKG inequality, which for Ising spins says that increasing functions of the configuration are positively correlated [@fkg-1971], and from the monotone coupling that it implies. What it does not follow from is where the transition is. Every inequality below is preserved if the couplings are replaced by any other ferromagnetic system with the same total mass, so no argument of this kind can distinguish the intensities at which the model is ordered — and this is not a gap in the exposition but a feature of monotonicity, which is why the wiki records the split. The threshold is located by the recursion, and the statement that above it the model is magnetised is that of Bleher and Sinai [@bleher-sinai-1973] [@bleher-sinai-1975], recorded here as the one external theorem the section on the threshold relies on. The order parameter is the number this article is about. It is defined from the plus state, it is positive exactly when there are two phases, it bounds the correlation from below, and monotonicity gives one weak upper bound on it and no lower one. title: The renormalisation group map
subtitle: Decimation as an operator on one-variable laws, and the scaling that makes it autonomous.
summary: Block decimation sends the law of a child's block spin to the law of the parent's: a nonlinear operator on probability measures on the line, a Gibbs tilt of a product measure followed by summation. Rescaling the spin by L to the power minus (d+alpha)/2 makes the operators at different scales into powers of a single map, whose fixed points and linearisations carry the critical behaviour.
text: Block decimation turns the exact recursion of a hierarchical spin system into an operator $\mathcal T_b$ on probability measures on the line: take $m$ independent copies of a law, tilt them by $\exp(b\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'})$, and record the law of their sum. The model applies $\mathcal T_{\beta J_n}$ with $J_n$ decaying geometrically, so the sequence of operators is not autonomous; rescaling the spin by $L^{-\theta}$ with $\theta=\tfrac12(d+\alpha)$ multiplies the coupling by $L^{2\theta}$ at each step and makes the composition a power of one map $\mathcal R_\theta$. That map is the object whose fixed points, and whose linearisation at them, carry the critical behaviour: a fixed point is a self-similar block-spin law, and the eigenvalues of the derivative there are the exponents, in the way made precise in the article on exponents . The recursion for that variance is fractional linear, so it is solved in closed form: the block-spin variance at scale $n$ is $L^{dn}$ divided by $1-\beta\sum_{x\ne0}J(\lVert x\rVert)$ truncated to the first $n$ shells. Three consequences follow without further work. The critical intensity is the reciprocal of the total kernel mass, so the interaction is summable exactly in the regime in which the intensity is finite; the susceptibility is exactly $(\beta_c-\beta)^{-1}\beta_c$; and the recursion written in the dimensionless variable $u_n=\beta J_nv_n$ has a nonzero fixed point whose multiplier is $L^\alpha$. The multiplier is the point of the exercise. In the dictionary of the exponent article , a multiplier $\lambda_1=L^\alpha$ at the critical fixed point gives $\nu=\log L/\log\lambda_1=1/\alpha$, which is the classical long-range value; together with the block-spin growth exponent $\theta=\tfrac12(d+\alpha)$, which the normalisation of the recursion at the autonomous scale forces, it gives $\kappa=\alpha$ and hence $\eta=2-\alpha$. These are the values tabulated for long-range interactions by Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972], and they are exact for this model. The Gaussian model is the one case of the hierarchical recursion that is solved in closed form, and it is the reference point for the others: the non-Gaussian fixed point of Bleher and Sinai merges with it at $\alpha=d/2$ and governs the critical behaviour above that value, and the percolation exponents of the percolation article coincide with the Gaussian ones in the sense that its two-point exponent is also $2-\alpha$. subtitle: Why the quartic coupling is relevant above half the dimension, and what it is a computation of.
summary: At the Gaussian fixed point the linearised decimation map is triangular in the basis of even monomials, and its diagonal entries are L^(d(1-k)+k alpha) for the monomial of degree 2k. The first entry is the variance multiplier; the second is the eigenvalue of the quartic coupling, which exceeds one exactly when alpha exceeds half the dimension. The relevance of the quartic term, the crossover at alpha = d/2 and the upper critical dimension four of the nearest-neighbour model are therefore one computation.
text: The Gaussian renormalisation group computes one eigenvalue: the variance of the block spin is multiplied by $L^{\alpha}$ per scale at the critical point, and that gives $\nu=1/\alpha$. That is the first of a family. At the Gaussian fixed point the linearised map is triangular in the basis of even monomials, and the monomial $s^{2k}$ carries the eigenvalue $$\lambda_{2k}=L^{\,d(1-k)+k\alpha},$$ of which the variance direction is $k=1$. The next one, $\lambda_4=L^{2\alpha-d}$, is the eigenvalue of the quartic coupling, and it exceeds one exactly when $\alpha>d/2$. So the statement that the quartic coupling is irrelevant below half the dimension, which the truncations article and the fixed-point article both rely on, is not an extra input: it is the second diagonal entry of the same matrix. The formula also reproduces the familiar thresholds. A nearest-neighbour model has $\alpha=2$ in this language, and then $\lambda_4=L^{4-d}$: marginal at $d=4$, relevant below it, irrelevant above. That is the upper critical dimension, and the crossover at $\alpha=d/2$ is the same equation $\lambda_4=1$ read in the other variable. The classical long-range exponent values and the threshold are those of Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972]; what this article adds is that in the hierarchical model they follow from the linearisation by a computation short enough to give in full. Two limits on the statement are worth naming at the outset. It is a statement about the Gaussian fixed point, so it says when that fixed point is unstable, not what replaces it; the replacement is the subject of the Bleher-Sinai article . And it is a statement about finite-dimensional truncations of the space of perturbations, triangular in the monomial basis; the eigenvalues of the full map on a Banach space of interactions require the analytic estimates of the rigorous analyses. title: Critical exponents from the renormalisation group
subtitle: Two numbers from the fixed point, and the algebra that turns them into the exponents.
summary: The exponents of a hierarchical model are read off from its fixed point: one from the multiplier of the linearised map, giving the correlation-length exponent, and one from the growth of the block spin, giving the susceptibility exponent and hence the two-point exponent. The growth exponent itself is then proved to be alpha at criticality, with the normalised second moment bounded away from zero and from infinity, from a two-child comparison, a runaway argument for the upper bound and a trapping argument for the amplitude. What is not proved is the pointwise decay of the two-point function, which for the percolation class on the same lattice is a theorem. summary: For kernel exponent above half the dimension the critical orbit of the hierarchical recursion converges to a self-similar law that is not Gaussian: the fixed point of Bleher and Sinai and of Gawedzki and Kupiainen. summary: Near a fixed point the orbit approaches along the stable directions, so every power law carries corrections from the second eigenvalue. In the hierarchical model the corrections are geometric in the scale and therefore pure powers of the correlation length, one for each subleading eigenvalue, with exponent omega equal to minus the logarithm of the subleading eigenvalue over the logarithm of the scale; a complex pair makes them oscillate in the logarithm of the length, and an eigenvalue tending to one makes them logarithmic.

title: The free energy and its singularity
subtitle: The recursion summed scale by scale, the Gaussian case in closed form, and where the curvature diverges.
summary: The free energy of a hierarchical model is a sum over scales, one elementary term per decimation step, and for a Gaussian prior each term is a Gaussian integral in closed form. That gives the free energy of the Gaussian model as an explicit series, convergent exactly up to the critical intensity, and a curvature that diverges there. The same computation gives the classical specific-heat exponent by a scaling argument, and the argument shows why the Ising case, where no term is elementary, cannot be treated this way.
text: The decimation article proves that the free energy per site converges, $F=\lim_nF_n$, and that it is convex in the intensity. It does not say what $F$ is, or what happens to it at the critical intensity, and those are the two questions this article answers for the one case in which they can be answered by computation. The mechanism is the per-scale decomposition. Each decimation step contributes one term to $F$, the logarithm of an expectation taken over $m$ independent copies of the block spin one scale down; for a Gaussian prior that expectation is an integral of a quadratic form, and for a Gaussian vector the sum of the components and the sum of their squares are independent. So the term is a product of two one-dimensional Gaussian integrals, and the whole free energy is an explicit series. title: Koch and Wittwer's non-Gaussian fixed point
subtitle: Convergent expansions for a fixed point with unbounded spins, large fields included.
summary: Koch and Wittwer proved the existence of a non-Gaussian fixed point of the hierarchical renormalisation map, in the hierarchical approximation of the three-dimensional phi-fourth fixed point, by a method that treats the large-field region: Borel summation brings the region where the perturbative expansion fails back into it, so that the theory is described by convergent expansions. The companion papers study the transformation itself, with its beta function and the relation between Dyson's and Gallavotti's hierarchies, and treat the Dyson-Baker hierarchy.
text: A fixed point of the hierarchical renormalisation map that is not quadratic is the critical theory of the scalar model above the marginal exponent, and the two general routes to it leave a gap. The theorem of Bleher and Sinai proves existence in a class of measures, but its statement is qualitative and its hypotheses are those of a parameter range; the epsilon expansion of Gawedzki and Kupiainen describes a neighbourhood of the marginal exponent. Koch and Wittwer closed the gap for the hierarchical model with unbounded spins by proving that the non-Gaussian fixed point governing the infrared behaviour of the three-dimensional critical theory exists, and that the theory around it is described by convergent expansions [@koch-wittwer-1986]. The obstacle they had to remove is the large-field problem . With a phi-fourth single-spin distribution the spins are unbounded, and the region in which the field is large carries most of the measure while lying outside the reach of the perturbative expansion; a renormalisation-group argument that controls the small-field region alone does not define the map. Their method handles that region by Borel summation, which resums the perturbation series so that the large-field region is incorporated into the perturbative one, and improves on the analyticity techniques of Gawedzki and Kupiainen's hierarchy-model papers [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1982] [@gawedzki-kupiainen-tirozzi-1984]. The result is a fixed point with a convergent expansion around it, at a specific parameter value and without a small parameter. The two companion papers complete the picture. The paper of 1991 studies the renormalisation transformation for scalar hierarchical models as an object in its own right: the beta function written for the transformation, its asymptotic behaviour, and the connection between the hierarchical models of Dyson and of Gallavotti [@koch-wittwer-1991]. The paper of 1994 proves a nontrivial fixed point for the Dyson-Baker hierarchical model, the variant whose blocks come from an expanding map of the interval [@koch-wittwer-1994]. The model is the hierarchical approximation of a three-dimensional lattice field theory with a phi-fourth interaction: the block sums of the hierarchy play the role of the block averages of the lattice, and the fixed point of the map is the critical theory of the approximation. A fixed point is a potential $V^*$ with $\mathcal V_bV^*=V^*$ up to an additive constant, and the problem is to find one that is not quadratic. The quadratic fixed point exists for exactly one curvature at each coupling, is computed in the Gaussian article , and is the fixed point that loses stability at the marginal exponent; the non-quadratic fixed point is the one that takes over. Because the single-spin distribution has unbounded support, the domain of the map is not a space of bounded functions: the tilt and the constraint allow configurations in which one child carries an arbitrarily large spin, and the integral defining $\mathcal V_bV$ is finite only because the prior decays. title: Abdesselam's trajectory between two fixed points
subtitle: A whole orbit of the renormalisation group, from the Gaussian fixed point to the nontrivial one.
summary: A fixed point describes one scale-invariant theory; a trajectory between two fixed points describes the whole crossover from the ultraviolet to the infrared. Abdesselam constructed such a trajectory rigorously and nonperturbatively for a three-dimensional phi-fourth model with modified propagator, joining the Gaussian fixed point to an analogue of the Wilson-Fisher fixed point, by a fixed point argument in a Banach space of sequences which perturbs a nonlinear one-dimensional iteration.
text: The renormalisation group of a lattice field theory is a map on a space of interactions, one step per scale, and most rigorous results about it are local: a fixed point, its stable and unstable manifolds, and the behaviour of orbits near it. A complete trajectory is a global object instead, an orbit defined at every scale and asymptotic at one end to the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point and at the other to the nontrivial infrared one. Abdesselam constructed such a trajectory rigorously and nonperturbatively for the three-dimensional $\varphi^4$ model with a modified free propagator [@abdesselam-2007], joining the Gaussian fixed point to an analogue of the Wilson-Fisher fixed point of the kind constructed by Brydges, Mitter and Scoppola [@brydges-mitter-scoppola-2003]. Two features of the construction matter for this wiki. It does not use the hierarchical approximation — the map is the Euclidean one — and yet the unperturbed problem it perturbs is a nonlinear one-dimensional iteration of exactly the kind the hierarchical model provides, with the perturbation supplied by the modified propagator [@abdesselam-2009]. The hierarchical recursion is therefore not an analogy for the Euclidean renormalisation group in this work but its first approximation, and the trajectory is recovered from the one-dimensional flow by a fixed-point argument in a space of sequences of effective potentials. The modification of the propagator is what makes the argument close: it suppresses the fluctuations at each scale by a fixed amount, so that the Euclidean step is a bounded perturbation of the hierarchical one. Whether the trajectory can be transported to the unmodified propagator is a separate question, and the construction is a statement about the modified model. Definitions and setting # The renormalisation group is the following operation, in the form used in the renormalisation-group treatment of lattice fields [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. One fixes a fluctuation covariance $C$, a positive definite kernel on the lattice, and a decomposition of it into pieces $C=\sum_jC_j$ indexed by scale. Given an effective potential $V_j$ at scale $j$, one defines $$e^{-V_{j+1}(\varphi)}=\int e^{-V_j(\varphi+\zeta)}\,\mu_{C_j}(d\zeta),$$ the convolution of the Boltzmann weight with the Gaussian measure of covariance $C_j$, followed by the rescalings of field and position that put the result in a fixed normal form. The map $V_j\mapsto V_{j+1}$ is the renormalisation step, and a fixed point of the step is a scale-invariant theory. A trajectory between two fixed points is a sequence $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ of effective potentials, each in the domain of the map, such that $V_{j+1}$ is the image of $V_j$ for every $j$, and such that $V_j$ converges to the Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. The first limit is the ultraviolet, the second the infrared; the intermediate potentials describe the crossover, which is the region in which neither fixed point's linearisation controls the flow. For the hierarchical model the corresponding object is a sequence of laws $\nu_j=\mathcal R_{\theta_0,b}^{\,j}\nu_0$ under the single map of the autonomous form , and a trajectory between fixed points is an orbit whose two ends are the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points of that map. In that case the trajectory is a property of a one-dimensional iteration and can be analysed by the methods of the fixed-point article . Then there is a sequence of effective potentials $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ satisfying the renormalisation recursion exactly, asymptotic to the ultraviolet Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial infrared fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. title: The fixed points, and what is known about each
subtitle: An inventory of the fixed points of the hierarchical recursion, what they share, and what distinguishes them.
summary: The recursion of a hierarchical model has few fixed points and they can be listed. There is the trivial law at the origin, a one-parameter Gaussian family of which the critical member is the standard normal, a nontrivial law whose existence is Bleher and Sinai's theorem and whose spectrum is known, and above criticality only degenerate laws on two points. At every fixed point with a finite nonzero variance the growth exponent is the same, theta = (d+alpha)/2, so the susceptibility exponent is alpha everywhere; what varies from one fixed point to another is the multiplier of the linearisation, hence the correlation-length exponent, and the subleading spectrum, hence the corrections. The article collects the statements, says which are proved and by which argument, and records the marginal cases in which two of the fixed points coalesce.

The renormalisation group of a hierarchical model is one operator on laws on the line, and the theory of the model is the study of its orbits. This article is the inventory: what the fixed points are, which of them are proved to exist and by which argument, what they have in common, and what distinguishes them. It adds no analysis of its own beyond the assembling; every statement is proved or attributed in the article it links to, and the tables say which. The organising fact is a division of labour that is easy to miss when the exponents are read off one fixed point at a time. title: Renormalisation for hierarchical percolation
subtitle: Cluster amplification is the relevant direction, and the triangle threshold is three alpha against d.
summary: For long-range percolation on the hierarchical lattice the renormalisation group acts on clusters rather than on a one-variable law, and its relevant direction is the amplification of large clusters across a block. The critical two-point function decays like the distance to the power minus d minus alpha for every exponent in the long-range range, and the triangle diagram converges exactly when three alpha is below d, which is where the model stops being mean-field.
text: Long-range percolation on the hierarchical lattice has bond intensities $J\lVert x-y\rVert^{-d-\alpha}$, so the intensity of the edge between two vertices depends only on their level, and the model inherits the child decomposition of the lattice. Its renormalisation group does not act on the law of one number: the state of a block is the partition of its vertices into clusters, and the operation of decimation is the passage from the cluster partition of the children to that of the block. What survives from the spin case is the amplification: two large clusters in sibling blocks are joined with probability comparable to $\beta J_n$ times their product of sizes, so a block whose clusters are atypically large produces a parent whose clusters are larger still. That mechanism gives the exact exponents. At criticality the expected size of the restricted cluster of the origin in $\Lambda_n$ grows like $L^{\alpha n}$ — the growth exponent $\kappa=\alpha$ of the exponent dictionary — and the critical connection probability between vertices at distance $L^n$ is of order $L^{-(d-\alpha)n}$, so $\eta=2-\alpha$ for every $0<\alpha<d$. This is unambiguous in the mean-field region, where the second moment of the cluster size diverges, and it holds beyond it as well; the theorem is Hutchcroft's, and it is the only case in which the two-point exponent is known across the whole long-range range [@hutchcroft-hierarchical-2021]. The phase transition itself is classical: $\beta_c$ is finite exactly when $\alpha<d$, and there is no infinite cluster at $\beta_c$ [@koval-meester-trapman-2012]. The renormalisation group enters at the level of exponents, and the question it answers is why the model is mean-field below $\alpha=d/3$ and not above: the triangle diagram is a convergent sum below that value and a divergent one above it, and the diagram is computable here because the lattice is ultrametric. title: The volume of the critical cluster
subtitle: The exponent delta, its value in each range of the dimension, and why the two-point function does not give it.
summary: The two-point function at criticality controls connections between pairs of vertices; the volume of the cluster of a vertex is a different observable, and the exponents that govern it are not read off the two-point function. In hierarchical long-range percolation the volume exponent is known exactly in every regime: the tail of the cluster volume decays like n to the minus (d-alpha)/(d+alpha) below the upper critical dimension d = 3 alpha, like n to the minus one half above it, and with a specific polylogarithmic correction at the dimension itself. The triangle threshold is where the two behaviours meet, and the log correction there agrees with neither of the predictions for the Euclidean model.
text: The percolation article derives two exponents from the critical two-point function: it decays like the distance to the power $-(d-\alpha)$, so $\eta=2-\alpha$, and the block susceptibility grows like $L^{\alpha n}$, so $\kappa=\alpha$. Those are statements about pairs. The volume of a cluster is a statement about a set, and the two are related only through the scaling relations, which are not theorems about any particular model. This article is about the set. The two thresholds of the percolation model should not be confused with the two marginal exponents of the spin model. The triangle threshold $3\alpha=d$ is a property of the percolation class alone; the summability threshold $\alpha=d$ decides whether the model is a Gibbs system at all, and the quartic threshold $\alpha=d/2$ is a property of the spin model's linearisation. subtitle: With a vector spin the block direction does not settle at criticality, and the marginal exponent is decided by a slowly varying factor.
summary: For the r-component hierarchical model the decimation map acts on laws on R^r by the same tilt, and it commutes with rotations. Bleher and Major proved Dyson's conjecture for this model: at the marginal kernel exponent a transition exists exactly when the level couplings are not summable, the spontaneous magnetisation vanishes at the critical temperature, and the normalised average spin still converges to the uniform law on the sphere. At the critical temperature the direction of the block spin does not concentrate: Bleher and Major proved that the normalised average spin converges in law to the uniform distribution on the sphere, while the spontaneous magnetisation vanishes [@bleher-major-2021]. The same work settles Dyson's conjecture for this model at the marginal exponent. When $\alpha=d$ the interaction is summable or not according to the level sequence: $\sum_nJ_nL^{dn}=\sum_nl_n$. subtitle: The recursion is an integral operator on potentials; the Gaussian truncation is exact and every other truncation leaks.
summary: Written on potentials rather than on laws, the decimation step is an explicit integral operator: the effective potential of a block is minus the logarithm of a constrained convolution of the child potential. Quadratic potentials are mapped to quadratic potentials and the flow on them is the fractional linear recursion for the variance; quartic and higher truncations are not invariant, because the constrained average of a quartic generates powers of every even order. The two rigorous treatments of the resulting infinite-dimensional flow are Koch and Wittwer's fixed point and, in the Euclidean setting, the trajectory of Abdesselam.
text: In the hierarchical model with a spin prior of the form $e^{-V(s)}ds$ the state of the recursion is a potential, not a number: after one decimation step the block spin has a density whose negative logarithm is the effective potential , computed from the child potential by a constrained convolution. The recursion is exact and it is an operation on an infinite-dimensional space; the question is which finite-dimensional families it leaves invariant, and the answer is that only the quadratic one does. Write $V(s)=\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2+\lambda s^4$; the Gaussian part flows by a fractional linear recursion solved in the Gaussian article , and the quartic part generates powers of every even order, so a two-coupling truncation is an approximation whose error is not controlled by the recursion itself [@bleher-sinai-1973]. The two rigorous treatments of the full flow are Koch and Wittwer's proof of a nontrivial fixed point for scalar hierarchical models [@koch-wittwer-1986], described in this wiki's article on it , and, in the Euclidean setting, Abdesselam's construction of a complete trajectory between the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points [@abdesselam-2007], described in the article on that . The hierarchical recursion is the one-dimensional iteration which Abdesselam's construction perturbs, so the potential formulation of this article is where the two meet. The quartic coupling is relevant exactly when the kernel exponent is above half the dimension, which is the hierarchical form of the upper critical dimension: for $\alpha<d/2$ the interaction is long enough that the Gaussian fixed point governs, and for $\alpha>d/2$ the nontrivial fixed point does. The values $\alpha=d/2$ and, for short-range models, $d=4$, are the same statement in the parametrisation of Fisher, Ma and Nickel [@fisher-ma-nickel-1972], and in this model the relevance of the quartic coupling is the second diagonal entry of the linearisation at the Gaussian fixed point, computed in the spectrum article . The hierarchical model with prior $e^{-V(s)}ds$ has the decimation recursion of the decimation article , and its block-spin law has a density because the tilt and the convolution of a density are densities. For $b\geq0$ the effective potential $\mathcal V_bV$ is defined by $$e^{-(\mathcal V_bV)(s)}=\frac{1}{Z_b(V)}\int_{\mathbb R^{m-1}}\exp\Bigl(b\sum_{a<a'}s_as_{a'}\Bigr)\prod_{a=1}^{m-1}e^{-V(s_a)}\,ds_1\cdots ds_{m-1},$$ with $s_m=s-\sum_{a<m}s_a$, and the scaled potential at exponent $\theta$ is $(\mathcal R_\theta V)(s)=(\mathcal V_bV)(L^{\theta}s)$ up to an additive constant. The potential formulation and the law formulation of the map article carry the same information: $e^{-(\mathcal V_bV)}$ is the density of $\mathcal T_b(e^{-V}ds)$. The constant in front is fixed by normalisation and plays no role in the flow of the shape of the potential; additive constants are the free energy increments of the free energy recursion and are dropped from the potential from here on. The Gaussian truncation # The one family the recursion preserves is the quadratic one, and on it the recursion is explicit. Let $V(s)=\tfrac{\mu}{2}s^2$ with $\mu>0$ and $b<1/(v(m-1))$, where $v=1/\mu$. Then $\mathcal V_bV$ is quadratic, with curvature $\mu'$ given by $$\frac{1}{\mu'}=\frac{m}{\mu-b(m-1)},$$ that is $\mu'=(\mu-b(m-1))/m$: the curvature flows affinely, and the variance recursion $v'=mv/(1-bv(m-1))$ is the same statement for $v=1/\mu$. title: The two marginal exponents
subtitle: Alpha equal to d decides summability, alpha equal to d/2 decides relevance, and they are not the same threshold.
summary: Two values of the kernel exponent are distinguished in the hierarchical model and they are easy to conflate. At alpha equal to d the interaction stops being summable and the level sequence alone decides whether the model is a Gibbs system with a transition. At alpha equal to d/2 the quartic coupling is marginal at the Gaussian fixed point, so the nontrivial fixed point is relevant above that value and the classical exponents hold below it. The first threshold is about the measure, the second about the map; one is a criterion at a point, the other a bifurcation.

title: Hierarchical and Euclidean renormalisation
subtitle: Why the recursion closes here, what fails on the lattice, and how the model is used anyway.
summary: The hierarchical recursion is exact because a block has no boundary: all pairs between two children carry one coupling, so the decimated state is a function of the child states alone. On the Euclidean lattice a block has a boundary of codimension one, the effective interaction after decimation depends on the geometry of the boundary and not on block sums, and the decimated measure need not be Gibbsian. The hierarchical model is nevertheless the reference for power counting, for the epsilon expansion and for the local analysis of the renormalisation map.
text: The decimation identity is an identity, and not an approximation, because of one geometric fact: any two vertices in different children of a hierarchical block are at the same distance, so every pair joining two children carries the same coupling and the interaction between them is a function of the two block sums. A block has no boundary in the sense that no pair of its vertices is closer to the outside than another, and its children are congruent copies of itself. The recursion therefore closes on the law of one number. On $\mathbb Z^d$ none of this holds. A cube of side $L^n$ has a boundary of codimension one: the fraction of pairs at distance of order $L^n$ that join two neighbouring blocks is small, the number of nearest-neighbour edges crossing the boundary is of order $L^{(d-1)n}$ rather than $L^{dn}$, and the interaction between two blocks depends on whether they share a face, an edge or a corner. After one decimation step the effective interaction between two block magnetisations is a sum over a boundary whose size depends on the pair, and after two steps the interaction acquires a dependence on the shape of the interface. There is no finite-dimensional family of interactions closed under the operation, and there is a stronger obstruction: the decimated measure of a Gibbs measure need not be Gibbsian at all [@van-enter-fernandez-sokal-1993]. What the hierarchical model supplies in spite of this is the local structure of the renormalisation map itself: its fixed points, the dimension of the unstable manifold, the eigenvalue problem, the $\varepsilon$-expansion about the upper critical exponent, and the mechanism by which the nonlinearity is irrelevant [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1983]. Those are the inputs of the Euclidean renormalisation group, and the hierarchical model is the setting in which they can be established; the transfer is the programme of Gawedzki and Kupiainen for lattice field theory [@gawedzki-kupiainen-1980], and of the renormalisation-group analysis of critical $(\Phi^4)_3$ and related models [@brydges-mitter-scoppola-2003] [@bauerschmidt-brydges-slade-2019]. Definitions and setting # Let $L\geq2$. On the hierarchical lattice the level-$n$ block is the subgroup $\Lambda_n$ of the lattice article , its children are the cosets of $\Lambda_{n-1}$, and the decimation state at level $n$ is the law of the block spin $S_{\Lambda_n}$. On $\mathbb Z^d$ the level-$n$ block at $x$ is the cube $x+[0,L^n)^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$, its children are the $L^d$ subcubes of side $L^{n-1}$, and the decimation state at level $n$ is the joint law of the $L^d$ block magnetisations of the children together with the fine configuration inside them. An interaction is a function $\Phi$ on configurations; a decimation step maps the Gibbs measure with interaction $\Phi$ on the fine lattice to the law of the coarse variables. A family of interactions is closed if the decimated measure is again a Gibbs measure with an interaction in the family, for every member of the family and every choice of the coarse-graining scale. What closes the recursion # Suppose that a block $B$ is the disjoint union of $m$ children $B_1,\ldots,B_m$ and that the interaction is a sum over unordered pairs of a coupling that is constant on the set of pairs joining two given children. Then the energy of a configuration on $B$ is a function of the child configurations through the $m$ block sums alone, and the law of the $m$-tuple of block sums under the Gibbs measure of $B$ is determined by the interaction inside a child and by the $m(m-1)/2$ couplings between children. If in addition every child is isomorphic to $B$ with the same internal interaction, one decimation step is the map $\mathcal T_b$ of the map article , and the family of interactions on the scale of a block is closed. title: The block structure
subtitle: part 1
summary: Nested blocks, congruent children, and the decimation identity they make exact.
text: Six articles establish the object everything else rests on: a group whose balls are cosets of nested finite-index subgroups, with the same number of children at every scale. The child decomposition says that every pair of vertices in different children of a block sits at the top level of that block, which is what makes the energy split into the children plus one interaction between their sums. The decimation identity is that statement written as an identity for partition functions, and it is the whole reason the renormalisation group is exact here. The fourth article passes from the blocks to the lattice, where the two-point function and the phase live; the fifth isolates what the argument actually uses and carries it to the p-adic integers; and the sixth describes the phase diagram from monotonicity alone, ending where the recursion has to take over.

title: The renormalisation group
subtitle: part 2
summary: The map on block-spin laws, its fixed points, and the exponents read off them.
text: The part has one object: the rescaled decimation map on laws on the line, of which the model is an orbit. It builds the operator; solves it exactly in the Gaussian case, where the orbit closes on the variance; reads off a fixed point the two numbers that matter, the multiplier of the linearisation, which gives the correlation-length exponent, and the growth of the block spin, which the autonomy of the recursion fixes for every fixed point of this model; and turns them into the exponent dictionary by algebra. That dictionary is an if-then statement, and the article after it supplies the 'if' for the hierarchical Ising model, a nontrivial fixed point with a spectrum, which is the theorem of Bleher and Sinai. With the spectrum in hand the corrections to the power laws follow from the subleading eigenvalues; the second existence proof, Koch and Wittwer's, is valid without a small parameter; and the part closes with the flow described globally rather than near a single fixed point, and with an inventory of the fixed points themselves — which are proved to exist, what each one determines, and what is the same at all of them.

title: Percolation, vectors, and the Euclidean comparison
subtitle: part 3
summary: What changes when the order parameter is a set, a vector, or a field on Z^d.
text: The same block structure carries models that are not the scalar spin model, and each one changes something specific. Percolation replaces the block-spin law by a cluster partition, and the mechanism that survives is amplification: two large clusters in sibling blocks are joined at a rate proportional to the product of their sizes. Vector spins make the block spin a vector, so the direction becomes an observable, and at criticality it does not settle. The phi-fourth truncation is where the infinite-dimensionality of the flow shows up, and the Euclidean comparison is where the exactness is lost.

The construction is nonperturbative, it does not use the hierarchical approximation, and its unperturbed problem is nevertheless a one-dimensional iteration of the kind the hierarchical model supplies - which is why it belongs in this wiki. title: Bauerschmidt, Brydges and Slade: the method, and the four-dimensional case
subtitle: reading map
text: This is the reading map for the one book in the catalogue that is not a paper: the Lecture Notes volume in which Roland Bauerschmidt, David Brydges and Gordon Slade develop their renormalisation group method, in the setting of the four-dimensional n -component |φ|⁴ model. The group is one work, so the map is not a survey of a literature; it says what the book is for, which parts of this wiki lean on it, and what it does not cover. The method is the one that made the four-dimensional case rigorous, and its organisation is worth knowing before opening the book. The renormalisation group is presented as a flow of potentials rather than of measures: one writes the effective potential after a decimation step as a sum of local polynomials, and the whole analysis is the control of the remainder under that flow. Two devices carry the control: a family of seminorms in which the flow is a contraction on the irrelevant directions, and a perturbation expansion whose terms are indexed by the scale at which they first appear. The book develops these for the hierarchical model first, because there the decimation step is an identity and the flow is a recursion on one variable; the Euclidean model is the target and the reason the machinery has to be as heavy as it is. title: Koch and Wittwer: the large-field problem
subtitle: reading map
text: This is the reading map for the three papers in which Hans Koch and Peter Wittwer proved that the hierarchical renormalisation map has a nontrivial fixed point with unbounded spins. The group is small and unusually homogeneous: the same two authors, one object, four papers, and a method that is the reason the papers are cited. The method is not a numerical certification. It is an analytic treatment of the large-field region , the part of the integral defining the effective potential in which the spin is too large for the perturbative expansion to converge and which, for an unbounded single-spin distribution, carries a non-negligible part of the measure. Borel summation resums the series there and brings the region back inside a convergent expansion. The point of the group, for this wiki, is that it closes the gap between the two other general treatments: the theorem of Bleher and Sinai gives existence in a class of measures with a qualitative statement and a parameter range, and the epsilon expansion of Gawedzki and Kupiainen describes a neighbourhood of the marginal exponent. Koch and Wittwer prove the fixed point of the hierarchical approximation of the three-dimensional theory, with convergent expansions around it, without a small parameter. title: Ultrametricity, nested blocks and exact shell counts
subtitle: proposition M8ZR
text: The level is subadditive under addition, $\operatorname{lev}(u+v)\leq\max\{\operatorname{lev}(u),\operatorname{lev}(v)\}$, and invariant under negation. Consequently $\lVert x-z\rVert\leq\max\{\lVert x-y\rVert,\lVert y-z\rVert\}$ for all $x,y,z$, the distance is symmetric and translation invariant, and $\lVert x\rVert=0$ only at $x=0$. Each $\Lambda_n$ is a subgroup, the blocks of a fixed level are its cosets, and two blocks are disjoint or one contains the other. Finally $$\lvert\Lambda_n\rvert=L^{dn}=m^n,\qquad \bigl\lvert\{x:\operatorname{lev}(x)=n\}\bigr\rvert=L^{dn}-L^{d(n-1)}\quad(n\geq1).$$ Proof of ultrametricity and the counts Let $u,v\in\mathbb H^d_L$ and $k=\max\{\operatorname{lev}(u),\operatorname{lev}(v)\}$. Both vanish above coordinate $k$, hence so does $u+v$, and $\operatorname{lev}(u+v)\leq k$; the coordinates of $-u$ are the negatives of those of $u$, so $\operatorname{lev}(-u)=\operatorname{lev}(u)$. Taking $u=x-y$ and $v=y-z$ gives the strong triangle inequality. Symmetry is $\operatorname{lev}(y-x)=\operatorname{lev}(x-y)$, translation invariance is $\operatorname{lev}((x+w)-(y+w))=\operatorname{lev}(x-y)$, and positive definiteness is the definition together with $\operatorname{lev}(x)\geq1$ for $x\neq0$. The condition $\operatorname{lev}(z)\leq n$ is exactly $z_i=0$ for $i>n$, and the set of such $z$ is closed under addition and negation, so $\Lambda_n$ is a subgroup; it is contained in $\Lambda_{n+1}$. title: The hierarchical lattices of different dimensions are the same group
subtitle: proposition W9TF
text: Let $d\geq1$ and $L\geq2$, and let $\psi:(\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d\to\mathbb Z/L^d\mathbb Z$ be a bijection taking $0$ to $0$. Applying $\psi$ in every coordinate gives a group isomorphism $\Psi:\mathbb H^d_L\to\mathbb H^1_{L^d}$ with $$\lVert\Psi(x)-\Psi(y)\rVert_{\mathbb H^1_{L^d}}=\lVert x-y\rVert_{\mathbb H^d_L}^{\,d}.$$ Proof of the distance identity The map $\psi(a)=\sum_{j=1}^da_jL^{j-1}$ is a bijection of the underlying sets fixing $0$, and applying it coordinatewise is a bijection of the direct sums. A vertex of $\mathbb H^d_L$ has level $k$ exactly when its last nonzero entry is the $k$-th, which the coordinatewise application preserves because level is read off the index and not the entry; a vertex of $\mathbb H^1_{L^d}$ at level $k$ has distance $(L^d)^k=L^{dk}$ from the origin and distance $L^k$ in the other lattice. Group structure is not needed for the distance identity, and it holds for $\Psi$ applied to a difference since the map is applied entrywise. The dimensional parameter is thus the ratio $\alpha/d$, which is why exponents in this model are functions of $\alpha/d$ and of the ratio of the kernel to the scale, and not of $d$ alone. subtitle: definition H8SN
text: A bijection $\phi:\mathbb H^d_L\to\mathbb H^d_L$ is an isometry if $\lVert\phi(x)-\phi(y)\rVert=\lVert x-y\rVert$ for all $x,y$, equivalently if $\operatorname{lev}(\phi(x)-\phi(y))=\operatorname{lev}(x-y)$. title: Translations and coordinate-wise bijections are isometries, and act transitively on levels
subtitle: theorem H3WQ
text: Translations are isometries, and so is every coordinate-wise bijection. Multiplying by $L^{-\theta}$ afterwards gives the second, since dilations commute. The identity is the reason no separate analysis is needed at each scale: a factor $\lambda$ in the spin is a factor $\lambda^2$ in the coupling, so the pair $(\text{scale},\text{coupling})$ flows on a cone.

title: The scalar fixed-point problem with unbounded spins
subtitle: definition C7QF
text: A fixed point is a potential $V^*$ with $\mathcal V_bV^*=V^*$ up to an additive constant, and the problem is to find one that is not quadratic. The quadratic fixed point exists for exactly one curvature at each coupling, is computed in the Gaussian article , and is the fixed point that loses stability at the marginal exponent; the non-quadratic fixed point is the one that takes over. Because the single-spin distribution has unbounded support, the domain of the map is not a space of bounded functions: the tilt and the constraint allow configurations in which one child carries an arbitrarily large spin, and the integral defining $\mathcal V_bV$ is finite only because the prior decays. The large-field region is the part of the domain of integration in which some $\lvert s_a\rvert$ exceeds a scale at which the perturbative expansion is valid, and controlling it is a precondition for the map to be defined at all as an operation on a space of potentials. ## Statement {#section-statement}

title: Trajectory between two fixed points
subtitle: definition D8WK
text: A trajectory between two fixed points is a sequence $(V_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z}$ of effective potentials, each in the domain of the map, such that $V_{j+1}$ is the image of $V_j$ for every $j$, and such that $V_j$ converges to the Gaussian fixed point as $j\to-\infty$ and to the nontrivial fixed point as $j\to+\infty$. The first limit is the ultraviolet, the second the infrared; the intermediate potentials describe the crossover, which is the region in which neither fixed point's linearisation controls the flow. For the hierarchical model the corresponding object is a sequence of laws $\nu_j=\mathcal R_{\theta_0,b}^{\,j}\nu_0$ under the single map of the autonomous form , and a trajectory between fixed points is an orbit whose two ends are the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points of that map. In that case the trajectory is a property of a one-dimensional iteration and can be analysed by the methods of the fixed-point article . ## Statement {#section-statement}

title: Existence of a complete trajectory in three dimensions
subtitle: theorem D4XR

text: Let $b>b_c$. Then $\mathcal R_{\theta,b}$ has no fixed point in $\mathcal E$, and the unrescaled orbit of the Ising initial law concentrates: the law of $S_n/m^n$ converges to the symmetric mixture $\tfrac12(\delta_{-M}+\delta_M)$, where $M=M(\beta)>0$ is the spontaneous magnetisation. Proof The concentration is part (ii) of the trichotomy : the orbit has unbounded variance after rescaling, and in the limit the block spin per site is $\pm M$, the two signs being the two phases of the magnetised-phase article . For a fixed point in $\mathcal E$ to exist at $b>b_c$ it would have to be fixed by $\mathcal R_{\theta_0,b}$ with a finite nonzero variance, and then the orbit of the Ising law would have to converge to it up to the relevant directions; but the orbit's variance per site grows like $m^{2n}$, so the rescaled variance diverges, and no limit in $\mathcal E$ exists. The only invariant laws of the unrescaled map consistent with concentration on $\pm M$ are $\delta_{\pm M}$ and their mixture, each of variance of order $m^{2n}$, which is outside $\mathcal E$. So the four kinds of the definition are exhaustive in the following sense: the rescaled map has fixed points in $\mathcal E$ only at $b\leq b_c$, and at $b=b_c$ the one it has is the nontrivial fixed point. title: One-edge joining of sibling clusters
subtitle: proposition P5CJ
text: Let $n\geq0$, let $B,B'$ be distinct children of $\Lambda_{n+1}$, let $x\in B$ and $y\in B'$, and let $I=\lvert K^{B}_x\rvert$ and $I'=\lvert K^{B'}_y\rvert$ computed with the bonds inside $B$ and $B'$ respectively. Then the pair $(I,I')$ is independent and $$\tau^{\Lambda_{n+1}}_\beta(x,y)\ \geq\ \mathbb E_\beta\bigl[1-e^{-\beta J_{n+1}II'}\bigr].$$ Proof of the one-edge bound Children are disjoint and every edge joining them is at level $n+1$, so the bonds of $B$ and of $B'$ are disjoint sets and $(I,I')$ is a pair of independent random variables, each with the law of the restricted cluster size in the model on $\Lambda_n$ with free boundary. Given $I=i$ and $I'=i'$, the $ii'$ pairs $\{u,v\}$ with $u$ in the cluster of $x$ and $v$ in the cluster of $y$ are distinct and their edges are independent of the internal bonds, each open with probability $1-e^{-\beta J_{n+1}}$. Any one open edge among them joins $x$ to $y$, so the conditional probability of connection is $1-(e^{-\beta J_{n+1}})^{ii'}=1-e^{-\beta J_{n+1}ii'}$. The inequality is the mechanism of amplification in one line: the probability of joining two clusters grows like $\beta J_{n+1}II'$ when the product is small, so an intensity decaying at rate $L^{-(d+\alpha)}$ is compensated by clusters growing at rate $L^{\alpha n}$, and a cluster size growing faster than $L^{\alpha n}$ produces

subtitle: definition RQEG
text: Write $\lvert K\rvert$ for the volume of the cluster of the origin, and define $\delta$ by $$\mathbb P_{\beta_c}\bigl(\lvert K\rvert\geq n\bigr)=n^{-1/\delta+o(1)},\qquad n\to\infty.$$ The upper critical dimension of the model is $d_c=3\alpha$: the value at which the triangle diagram of the percolation article changes from convergent to divergent, and the value at which the volume exponent changes value. subtitle: theorem B9HL
text: Let $r\geq2$, let the interaction be $U(x,y)=-l_nL^{-2n}\langle\sigma_x,\sigma_y\rangle$ at level $n$, and let the prior be uniform on $\mathbb S^{r-1}$. subtitle: definition 2I6O

title: The Euclidean block has a boundary and its decimation is not a function of block sums
subtitle: proposition Z7MR
text: Let $B=[0,L^n)^d\cap\mathbb Z^d$ with $n\geq1$ and $L\geq2$, and let $B_1,B_2$ be two subcubes of side $L^{n-1}$. The number of unordered pairs $\{x,y\}$ with $x\in B_1$, $y\in B_2$ is $L^{2d(n-1)}$, and the number of such pairs that are nearest neighbours is at most $dL^{d(n-1)}$. Moreover the fraction of nearest-neighbour edges of $\mathbb Z^d$ that join two distinct $L$-blocks equals $1/L$, independently of the scale. Proof of the boundary counts The two cubes each have $L^{d(n-1)}$ vertices, so there are $L^{2d(n-1)}$ unordered pairs. Each vertex has $2d$ neighbours, so the number of neighbouring pairs between the two cubes is at most $2dL^{d(n-1)}/2=dL^{d(n-1)}$: this is the bound for the count of pairs, and the exponent $d(n-1)$ against $2d(n-1)$ is the statement that only a fraction $L^{-d(n-1)}$ of the pairs are nearest neighbours. For the fraction of edges, count in the infinite lattice. Each block of the $L$-partition contains $L^d$ vertices; the nearest-neighbour edges with both endpoints in it are $dL^{d-1}(L-1)$, since there are $d$ directions and $L^{d-1}(L-1)$ edges in each. The number of edges per vertex of $\mathbb Z^d$ is $d$, so the number of edges per block is $dL^d$, and the fraction with both endpoints in the same block is $\frac{dL^{d-1}(L-1)}{dL^d}=\frac{L-1}{L}$. The crossing fraction is the complement, $1/L$. Two things follow. A decimation step on $\mathbb Z^d$ cannot be described by a handful of couplings between neighbouring block magnetisations,

title: Block-spin transformations can destroy the Gibbs property
subtitle: theorem Q2LN
text: There are translation-invariant Gibbs measures for finite-range lattice interactions whose image under a block-spin transformation is not a Gibbs measure for any interaction, and there are models for which the image is Gibbsian but with an interaction that is not absolutely summable. Consequently position-space decimation does not define a map on a space of interactions in general [@van-enter-fernandez-sokal-1993]. The reason is a long-range dependence in the coarse variables that is invisible in the fine ones: conditioning on the outside of a region in the coarse lattice constrains the fine configuration in a way that is not mediated by finitely many coarse variables, so the conditional probabilities of the coarse measure fail the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle form. The hierarchical model is immune because its coarse variables are the block sums and a block interacts with the rest of the lattice through its sum alone, so conditioning on the outside of a block constrains the block only through one number. ## Consequences and applications {#section-consequences} The reference model for the local analysis. The renormalisation map of a hierarchical model is a nonlinear map on a space of measures with exponential moments, and the analysis of its fixed points, its unstable manifold and the $\varepsilon$-expansion can be carried out completely, as in the Bleher–Sinai article . title: Figures and simulations
subtitle: 9 figures, 7 interactive
text: figures simulations The children of a level-2 block with $L=2$, $d=1$, with the pairs at each level drawn. The two-coupling truncation, with the Gaussian and nontrivial fixed points and the critical trajectory between them. One decimation step: the children, the tilt and the block spin. The classical exponents against the kernel exponent, with the crossover at $\alpha=d/2$ marked. The direction of the block spin below, at and above the critical intensity, which is the phenomenon of Bleher and Major. The coupling of a block to its complement: the field at one vertex, which decays, and its sum over the block, which grows below $\alpha=d$. The sampled cluster-size distribution on a block of 64 sites at three intensities, with the predicted slope as a guide. The Gaussian free energy per site and its curvature against the intensity, with the critical intensity marked. The cluster-volume exponent against the kernel exponent, mean field on one side of d = 3 alpha and (d+alpha)/(d-alpha) on the other. The Gaussian orbit of the variance recursion for a range of intensities, against the critical one. The exponent table over a grid of kernel exponents. The triangle diagram at criticality against its truncation level. The exact law of the block spin of sixteen sites, by enumeration. A heat bath for the Ising model on sixty-four sites. A percolation realisation on a block, drawn level by level. The exact block-spin laws of the plus, free and minus boundary conditions.
